name: Howard Aiken
milestone_by_age_26: Aiken was working as a power engineer at Westinghouse by age 26; his famous Harvard Mark I was not completed until 1944 when he was 44.
early_history_summary: Aiken earned his BS in electrical engineering from the University of Wisconsin in 1923, then worked as a power engineer at Westinghouse and other companies before entering Harvard as a graduate student in physics at age 33 in 1933. He conceived the idea for an automatic calculator around 1936 and completed the Mark I with IBM in 1944.
family_context_summary: Born in Hoboken, New Jersey; father came from a wealthy Indiana family but struggled with alcoholism, leading to family difficulties. Mother was the daughter of German immigrants.
evidence_summary: Aiken's path to computing was unusually late: he worked as a power engineer for nearly a decade before entering graduate school at 33. His landmark achievement, the Harvard Mark I, came at age 44. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Tom Kilburn
milestone_by_age_26: Co-designed and built the Manchester Baby, the world's first stored-program electronic digital computer, which successfully ran its first program on 21 June 1948.
early_history_summary: Kilburn was a mathematical specialist at Wheelwright Grammar School before winning multiple scholarships to Cambridge, where he graduated with First Class Honours in mathematics in 1942 via a shortened wartime course. During WWII he worked on radar at the Telecommunications Research Establishment under Freddie Williams, then was seconded to the University of Manchester in 1946 to continue their CRT storage work, leading directly to the Manchester Baby.
family_context_summary: Born in Earlsheaton, Dewsbury, Yorkshire; father was a statistical clerk at a wool mill who rose to company secretary. Mother stayed home to raise children. Working-class community with strong emphasis on education.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Father worked as a clerk at a wool mill, unrelated to engineering or computing.
primary_early_advantage_tags: elite grammar school, Cambridge scholarships, wartime radar lab, Williams mentorship, Manchester computing frontier
evidence_summary: Kilburn's path was shaped by elite institutional pipelines: a grammar school that nurtured his mathematical talent, scholarships to Cambridge, and wartime radar work at TRE under Freddie Williams. His sustained mentorship under Williams at TRE and then Manchester gave him direct access to the cutting edge of CRT storage technology. The complementary Williams-Kilburn partnership, combined with TRE resources and Manchester's position as a computing frontier, enabled the Baby by age 26. No family financial or domain advantage is documented.
starting_point: Born in Earlsheaton, Dewsbury, Yorkshire to a wool mill clerk turned company secretary and a stay-at-home mother; raised in a working-class Northern English mill town with strong parental emphasis on education.
current_position: Died on 17 January 2001 in Manchester at age 79; final role: Professor Emeritus of Computer Science at the University of Manchester, having led the development of five historically significant computers.

trajectory.event: Graduated from Cambridge with First Class Honours in mathematics and joined the Telecommunications Research Establishment to work on radar under Freddie Williams.
Co-developed the Williams-Kilburn tube for CRT storage at Manchester and published an influential internal report on binary digital storage in December 1947.
Co-designed and built the Manchester Baby, the world's first stored-program electronic digital computer, which ran its first program on 21 June 1948.
Led development of the Ferranti Mark 1, the world's first commercially available computer.
Led the development of the Atlas computer, one of the first time-sharing multiprocessing computers with paging and pipelining.
Became head of the Department of Computer Science at the University of Manchester.
Died on 17 January 2001 in Manchester after twenty years of quiet retirement.

name: Maurice Wilkes
milestone_by_age_26: Wilkes had completed his PhD and held a junior faculty position at Cambridge by age 26, but his landmark EDSAC computer was not built until 1949 when he was 35.
early_history_summary: Wilkes studied mathematics at St John's College, Cambridge from 1931, then did graduate work at the Cavendish Laboratory on radio wave propagation, earning his PhD in 1937. He was appointed university demonstrator at the newly created Mathematical Laboratory in 1937. After WWII service he returned to head the laboratory and built EDSAC, which began working in May 1949.
family_context_summary: Born in Dudley, Worcestershire, England. Interested in electronics as a boy and studied that subject in his spare time.
evidence_summary: Wilkes followed a standard academic path through Cambridge, earning his PhD at 24 and a junior faculty position at 24. His famous achievements—EDSAC, microprogramming, cache memories—all came after age 30. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Jay Forrester
milestone_by_age_26: Forrester was working on wartime servo control systems at MIT by age 26; his famous Whirlwind computer and magnetic core memory inventions came after age 29.
early_history_summary: Forrester grew up on a cattle ranch in Nebraska, earned his BS in electrical engineering from the University of Nebraska in 1939, and went to MIT as a graduate student. During WWII he designed servo control systems for radar on naval ships. He led the Whirlwind computer project from 1947, invented magnetic core memory in 1949, and later founded the field of system dynamics.
family_context_summary: Born on a cattle ranch near Climax, Nebraska; parents were homesteaders in one of the last areas of the plains to be settled. Mother taught him at home for his first two years; then he rode his horse to a one-room schoolhouse.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Father taught him in the one-room schoolhouse, suggesting a teaching role but no technical domain transfer.
evidence_summary: Forrester's early career was productive wartime engineering at MIT, but his landmark achievements—Whirlwind, core memory, system dynamics—all came after age 29. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: J. Presper Eckert
milestone_by_age_26: Co-designed and served as chief engineer of ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic digital computer, which was completed and publicly demonstrated in February 1946 at the University of Pennsylvania.
early_history_summary: Eckert was raised in a wealthy Philadelphia family, attended the prestigious William Penn Charter School, and spent afternoons at Philo Farnsworth's electronics lab while in high school. He transferred from Wharton to the Moore School of Electrical Engineering at Penn, where he worked on radar timing and improved the differential analyzer. He met John Mauchly in a 1941 defense training course and became chief engineer of the ENIAC project on his 24th birthday in April 1943.
family_context_summary: Born to a wealthy real estate developer father and a mother from an old Philadelphia Quaker family; raised in a large house in Germantown, driven to school by chauffeur. Family wealth provided access to elite private education and electronics facilities.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a wealthy real estate developer of Swiss German and Alsatian descent; no direct technical domain transfer documented, but family wealth provided access to elite education and Farnsworth's electronics lab.
primary_early_advantage_tags: wealthy family, elite private school, Farnsworth lab access, Moore School, Mauchly partnership, wartime computing demand
evidence_summary: Eckert benefited from significant family wealth: a real estate developer father, private school education, and access to Philo Farnsworth's electronics lab as a teenager. He placed second nationally on the math College Board exam and transferred to the Moore School, a frontier of early computing. His partnership with John Mauchly combined Eckert's electronics engineering skill with Mauchly's conceptual vision, and wartime demand for ballistic calculations provided the structural wave that funded ENIAC. By age 26, ENIAC was completed and publicly demonstrated.
starting_point: Born into a wealthy Philadelphia family; father was a real estate developer, mother from an old Quaker family; raised in Germantown with chauffeur-driven private school education and access to electronics labs.
current_position: Died on June 3, 1995 in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania at age 76; final role: co-founder of Eckert-Mauchly Computer Corporation and executive at Sperry Rand's UNIVAC division.

trajectory.event: Applied for his first patent on light modulating methods while at the Moore School of Electrical Engineering at Penn.
Appointed chief engineer of the ENIAC project at the Moore School, collaborating with John Mauchly on the first general-purpose electronic digital computer.
ENIAC was completed and publicly dedicated on February 15, 1946 at the University of Pennsylvania, acclaimed as a major computing breakthrough.
Co-founded the Eckert-Mauchly Computer Corporation to build the UNIVAC, the first commercial computer in the United States.
UNIVAC I was delivered to the U.S. Census Bureau, becoming the first commercially produced computer in the United States.
Received the National Medal of Science for his contributions to computing.
Died on June 3, 1995 in Bryn Mawr, Pennsylvania.

name: John Mauchly
milestone_by_age_26: Mauchly had completed his PhD in physics and started as a professor at Ursinus College by age 26, but his ENIAC work did not begin until his mid-30s.
early_history_summary: Mauchly attended Johns Hopkins University on a scholarship, initially studying engineering before transferring to physics, and received his PhD in physics in 1932 at age 25. He became a professor of physics at Ursinus College, where he developed an interest in weather prediction and computational methods. In 1941 he attended a defense training course at the Moore School, met Eckert, and proposed the idea for ENIAC.
family_context_summary: Born in Cincinnati, Ohio; grew up in Chevy Chase, Maryland. Father had a doctorate from the University of Cincinnati. Attended Johns Hopkins on a state scholarship.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father had a doctorate, suggesting an academic household, but no specific technical domain transfer is documented.
evidence_summary: Mauchly followed a standard academic path: PhD at 25, professorship at 26. His famous ENIAC work began at age 34 when he attended the Moore School defense training course in 1941. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Grace Hopper
milestone_by_age_26: Hopper held an MA from Yale and was teaching mathematics at Vassar College by age 26; her pioneering computing work began in 1944 when she was 37.
early_history_summary: Hopper graduated from Vassar College in 1928 with a BA in mathematics and physics, earned an MA from Yale in 1930, and began teaching at Vassar in 1931. She completed her PhD at Yale in 1934. She joined the Naval Reserve in 1943 and was assigned to the Harvard Mark I project in 1944, beginning her computing career at age 37.
family_context_summary: Born in New York City; father was an insurance broker, mother had a love of mathematics which she passed to Grace. Parents believed daughters should have the same quality education as their son.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother had a love of mathematics and passed it on, providing some early mathematical exposure, but no professional domain transfer is documented.
evidence_summary: Hopper's early career was purely academic mathematics: BA at 22, MA at 24, PhD at 28, teaching at Vassar. Her transformative computing career—Mark I, compilers, COBOL—began at age 37. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Anita Borg
milestone_by_age_26: Borg was working as a programmer by age 26 but had not yet completed her PhD or made any notable contribution; her influential work began after her 1981 PhD at age 32.
early_history_summary: Borg got her first programming job in 1969 at a small insurance company, teaching herself to program. She attended the University of Washington for two years, then studied at NYU, where she received her PhD in computer science in 1981 at age 32. She later founded Systers (1987) and the Grace Hopper Celebration of Women in Computing.
family_context_summary: Born in Chicago, Illinois; grew up in Palatine, Illinois, then Hawaii, and Mukilteo, Washington. Family traveled extensively during her childhood.
evidence_summary: Borg's early career was a slow start: self-taught programming at 20, then years of work before completing her PhD at 32. Her influential advocacy work (Systers, Grace Hopper Celebration, Institute for Women and Technology) all came after age 38. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Radia Perlman
milestone_by_age_26: Perlman held BS and MS degrees from MIT and was designing network protocols at BBN by age 26, but her famous Spanning Tree Protocol was not invented until the mid-1980s when she was in her early 30s.
early_history_summary: Perlman was introduced to programming in high school at Stevens Institute of Technology, then got a part-time job at MIT's AI Lab in 1971. She earned her BS (1973) and MS (1976) in mathematics from MIT. After leaving MIT's PhD program, she joined BBN Technologies to design network protocols, then moved to DEC in 1980 where she invented the Spanning Tree Protocol. She returned to MIT for her PhD in 1988.
family_context_summary: Born in Portsmouth, Virginia; grew up in Loch Arbour, New Jersey. Both parents worked as engineers for the US government—father on radar, mother as a computer programmer. She is Jewish.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were engineers: father worked on radar, mother was a mathematician turned computer programmer. Mother helped with math homework, providing early mathematical exposure.
evidence_summary: Perlman had strong early advantages—engineer parents, MIT education, AI Lab programming job at 19—but her landmark Spanning Tree Protocol was invented at DEC in the mid-1980s when she was in her early 30s. By age 26 she was a junior protocol designer at BBN with no independently verifiable milestone. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Sally Floyd
milestone_by_age_26: Floyd was working as a computer systems engineer for BART by age 26; her influential congestion control research began after her 1989 PhD at age 39.
early_history_summary: Floyd received a BA in sociology from UC Berkeley in 1971, then learned electronics at a community college and spent eight years as a computer systems engineer for BART's train control systems. She returned to graduate school at Berkeley in 1984, earning her MS (1987) and PhD (1989) in computer science. She co-invented Random Early Detection (RED) with Van Jacobson in 1993.
family_context_summary: Born in Charlottesville, Virginia. Not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Floyd took a non-traditional path: sociology BA, electronics certificate, then eight years as a BART systems engineer before returning to grad school at 34. Her landmark RED algorithm came at 43. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Van Jacobson
milestone_by_age_26: Jacobson was a research scientist at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory by age 26; his landmark TCP congestion control work was published in 1988 when he was 38.
early_history_summary: Jacobson studied modern poetry, physics, and mathematics at the University of Arizona, receiving a BS in mathematics and an MS in physics. He worked at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory from 1974 as a research scientist in the Real-time Controls Group, later leading the Network Research Group. His famous TCP/IP congestion control algorithms were published in 1988.
evidence_summary: Jacobson's early career was as a research scientist at LBL working on real-time controls. His transformative TCP/IP congestion control work came in 1988 at age 38. No material milestone by age 26 was found.

name: S. Keshav
milestone_by_age_26: Keshav completed his B.Tech at IIT Delhi with a Director's Gold Medal by approximately age 26, but his significant networking research and textbook came after his 1991 PhD.
early_history_summary: Keshav earned his B.Tech in Computer Science from IIT Delhi in 1986, winning the Director's Gold Medal for best all-round performance. He then went to UC Berkeley for his MS (1988) and PhD (1991) in computer science, working on congestion control. He joined Bell Labs and later became a professor at Cornell, then Waterloo, and currently Cambridge.
evidence_summary: Keshav's undergraduate achievement at IIT Delhi was notable, but his significant research contributions—congestion control thesis, networking textbook, companies founded—all came after his 1991 PhD at age 31. No material career milestone by age 26 was found.

name: Deborah Estrin
milestone_by_age_26: Estrin completed her PhD from MIT at age 25 and began as an assistant professor at USC at 26, but her pioneering sensor networks work began in the late 1990s when she was in her late 30s.
early_history_summary: Estrin entered UC Berkeley in 1977, graduated with a BS in EECS in 1980, then moved to MIT where she received her PhD in EECS in 1985 under Jerry Saltzer. She became an assistant professor at USC in 1986, received the NSF Presidential Young Investigator Award in 1987, and later moved to UCLA where she founded the Center for Embedded Networked Sensing (CENS) in 2001.
family_context_summary: Both parents had PhDs in Electrical Engineering from UW Madison and were academics. Eldest sister is an MD, middle sister has an MS in Computer Science from Stanford and is a serial entrepreneur.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were PhD-level academics in electrical engineering, providing a strong academic and technical household environment.
evidence_summary: Estrin had a fast academic track—PhD from MIT at 25, assistant professor at 26—but her landmark work in sensor networks and mobile health came in the late 1990s and 2000s. No material career milestone by age 26 was found; her early achievements were standard academic progression.
